notes: Re-judged after the fact-check rewrite. Chosen hook (option 0, 'HYUNDAI PLANS AN / AI DATA CENTER', claim). Sub-scores: clear in under 2 seconds 9 (plain words, subject-verb-object, every word easy for ESL readers; the 16-character lines fit the render with no overflow); curiosity 4 (flatter than the old 'SUPERCOMPUTER' version; it is a straight news statement and the cover image, lit halls, robot arms and a car, carries the intrigue); concrete name or number 6 (Hyundai is named, no number); promise kept 9 (the slide 2 text says 'AI data center' and 'plans', matching the cover word for word; 'PLANS' is honest because everything in the post is a plan; the image matches); reader stake 2 (none, acceptable). The rewrite fixes the overpromise I noted earlier: 'supercomputer' was a loose term only ZDNet Korea used, while 'AI data center' is the Korea Times wording and matches both articles. Trade-off is lost punch, but a flat, honest hook that fully matches the slides beats a stronger hook the slides do not back. Other options: option 1 ('AI COMPUTE ISN'T JUST CHATBOTS', myth-flip) names no company, uses the jargon word 'compute', and the slides never mention chatbots, so the myth is invented. Option 2 ('HYUNDAI: $6.7B FOR AN AI HUB', number) invites the misreading that the data center costs $6.7B, which neither article says (regional commitment per Korea Times, whole AI Valley project per ZDNet Korea). The chosen hook is the best of the three. hook_types labels are acceptable and none claims reader-impact. hook_pick_reason has an honest 'No reader-impact hook:' reason (the articles state no effect on everyday readers) and now also explains why 'SUPERCOMPUTER' was dropped. Slide 2 renders cleanly ('02 / 08', 8 dots, no overflow). Optional only: if a sharper line is wanted later, a name-plus-fact variant that the articles support (for example naming Saemangeum or the March 2027 groundbreaking) could add concreteness, but it is not needed to pass.
